idiom_name: factory-created hub: on(event, fn) / emit(event, payload)
implementation_notes: JavaScript needs no structure for Mediator: a small object or closure holding a Map from event name to an array of listener functions is the whole hub - colleagues register with on() and talk through emit() instead of importing each other, and the hub is created per composition and injected. Functions and duck typing replace the Colleague hierarchy, so nothing enforces the protocol; a single place for the event vocabulary (an object of constants, a JSDoc/TS union) keeps it readable. Reach for the EventEmitter variant when you want the bookkeeping (once, off, listener limits, error events) supplied, and for EventTarget when the hub should be a DOM-compatible target.
pitfalls: A hub kept at module scope with components that register on setup is the classic leak: listeners hold closures and their DOM nodes alive, so deregister on teardown or use AbortSignal/WeakRef.
emit is synchronous, so a throwing listener aborts the listeners after it and the caller; catch per listener in the hub or route failures through a dedicated event.
Unsubscribing during dispatch mutates the array being iterated; iterate a copy (as above) or the next listener is skipped.
Event names and payloads are unvalidated, so a typo registers a listener that never fires; keep the event vocabulary in one module.

variants.name: Node EventEmitter hub
variants.implementation_notes: In Node the hub is normally an EventEmitter: the mediator extends EventEmitter (or owns one), colleagues subscribe with hub.on(name, listener) and publish with hub.emit(name, payload), and the emitter owns the listener bookkeeping (once, off, listener limits, 'error' semantics). The fan-out layer is stdlib, so the Colleague role collapses into whoever calls emit; keep the hub injected per composition rather than exported as a module singleton. In browsers the same role is played by EventTarget with addEventListener and dispatchEvent.
pitfalls: Listeners run synchronously in registration order and their return values are ignored, so async work must be scheduled explicitly (queueMicrotask/setImmediate) and one throwing listener aborts the rest.
An 'error' event with no listener throws; use a dedicated event name for domain failures or always attach a handler.
Listeners are retained strongly and re-registering the same handler stacks duplicates, eventually raising MaxListenersExceededWarning; remove them on teardown.
